"""Proposer input recipes: named, versioned, deterministic context builders.

A *recipe* maps ``(unit id, source text, project root)`` to the text the proposer
prompt renders in place of the whole unit file (RFC-0007, "Inputs: a context pack,
not the whole file"). Recipes are the experiment's input factor, so each is pure
and deterministic: the same arguments always yield the same context, and the
recipe's ``ref`` (``name/vN``) is recorded on every property it helped propose
(`Provenance.recipe`). A shipped version's behaviour is immutable; change a recipe
by registering a new version.

The v1 recipes are single-file (they read only the source text; the project root
is part of the seam for the project-index recipes of RFC-0007 T1):

- ``baseline``: today's whole file, minus any ``main`` and the leading file-header
  comment (both leak the answer on ``examples/``).
- ``sighted``: the target function with its doc comment, plus the type and macro
  definitions it uses.
- ``blind``: ``sighted`` without the target body: its signature, doc comment, and
  only the definitions the *signature* uses, so nothing in the pack can be
  transcribed from the implementation.

The scan is lexical (comments, literals and directives masked), not a parse; it
reads the same text ESBMC will, and degrades by omission rather than guessing.
Only type and macro definitions are pulled in: objects the body reads (tables,
globals), callees, and a struct reachable only through a variable declaration are
out of scope for v1.

from __future__ import annotations

import re
from collections.abc import Callable
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

from forseti.esbmc import find_definition_brace, mask_comments
from forseti.esbmc.preprocessor import mask_string_literals
from forseti.unit_id import unit_id_symbol


class RecipeError(ValueError):
    """A recipe could not build its context (unknown name, or no such function)."""


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProposalContext:
    """The text a recipe built, and the recipe ``ref`` that built it."""

    recipe: str
    text: str


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Recipe:
    name: str
    version: str
    build: Callable[[str, str, Path], str]

    @property
    def ref(self) -> str:
        """The provenance label, e.g. ``"blind/v1"``."""
        return f"{self.name}/v{self.version}"


_COMMENT_OR_LITERAL_RE = re.compile(
    r'"(?:\\.|[^"\\\n])*"|\'(?:\\.|[^\'\\\n])*\'|(?P<comment>//(?:\\\n|[^\n])*|/\*.*?\*/)',
    re.DOTALL,
)
_DIRECTIVE_RE = re.compile(r"^[ \t]*#(?:\\\n|[^\n])*", re.MULTILINE)
_DEFINE_RE = re.compile(r"^[ \t]*#[ \t]*define[ \t]+(\w+)(?:\\\n|[^\n])*", re.MULTILINE)
_IDENT_RE = re.compile(r"[A-Za-z_]\w*")
_TAG_RE = re.compile(r"\b(?:struct|union|enum)\s+(\w+)\s*\{")
_FN_PTR_NAME_RE = re.compile(r"\(\s*\*\s*(\w+)\s*\)")
_TYPE_HEADS = frozenset({"typedef", "struct", "union", "enum"})
_ATTRIBUTE_RE = re.compile(r"__attribute__\s*\(\(.*?\)\)\s*$", re.DOTALL)
_FOLLOWING_WORD_RE = re.compile(r"\s*([A-Za-z_]\w*)")
_CONTINUATION_WORDS = frozenset(
    {"__attribute__", "__attribute", "__asm__", "__asm", "asm"}
)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class _Item:
    start: int
    end: int
    brace: int | None
    is_function: bool


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class _Definition:
    start: int
    end: int
    names: frozenset[str]
    uses: frozenset[str]
    text: str


def _blank(match: re.Match[str]) -> str:
    return re.sub(r"[^\n]", " ", match.group(0))


def _code_view(no_comments: str) -> str:
    """Comment-masked source with literals and directives blanked, offsets kept."""
    return _DIRECTIVE_RE.sub(_blank, mask_string_literals(no_comments))


def _is_function_head(head: str) -> bool:
    return _ATTRIBUTE_RE.sub("", head.rstrip()).rstrip().endswith(")")


def _starts_new_item(code: str, start: int, end: int) -> bool:
    """True when an identifier follows a top-level `)` that cannot continue it.

    Only a semicolon-less macro invocation (``DECLARE_THING(x)``) is followed by
    another declaration's first word; ``;``, ``{``, ``,``, ``=``, ``(`` and the
    attribute/asm keywords all continue the item instead.
    """
    follower = _FOLLOWING_WORD_RE.match(code, end)
    return (
        follower is not None
        and follower.group(1) not in _CONTINUATION_WORDS
        and not code.startswith("__attribute__", start)
    )


def _top_level_items(code: str) -> list[_Item]:
    """Top-level declarations/definitions of `code` as offset spans."""
    items: list[_Item] = []
    depth = 0
    start: int | None = None
    brace: int | None = None
    initialised = False
    for i, ch in enumerate(code):
        if start is None:
            if ch.isspace():
                continue
            start, brace, initialised = i, None, False
        if ch in "([{":
            if ch == "{" and depth == 0 and brace is None:
                brace = i
            depth += 1
        elif ch in ")]}":
            depth = max(depth - 1, 0)
            if depth or initialised:
                continue
            if ch == "}" and brace is not None and _is_function_head(code[start:brace]):
                items.append(_Item(start, i + 1, brace, True))
                start = None
            elif ch == ")" and _starts_new_item(code, start, i + 1):
                items.append(_Item(start, i + 1, None, False))
                start = None
        elif ch == "=" and depth == 0:
            initialised = True
        elif ch == ";" and depth == 0:
            items.append(_Item(start, i + 1, brace, False))
            start = None
    return items


def _enumerators(text: str) -> set[str]:
    names: set[str] = set()
    for match in re.finditer(r"\benum\b[^{;]*\{", text):
        depth, i = 1, match.end()
        part = ""
        while i < len(text) and depth:
            ch = text[i]
            depth += ch in "([{"
            depth -= ch in ")]}"
            if (depth == 1 and ch == ",") or depth == 0:
                found = _IDENT_RE.search(part)
                if found:
                    names.add(found.group())
                part = ""
            else:
                part += ch
            i += 1
    return names


def _declarator_names(tail: str) -> set[str]:
    """The name each comma-separated declarator in `tail` declares."""
    parts: list[str] = []
    depth, part = 0, ""
    for ch in tail:
        depth += ch in "(["
        depth -= ch in ")]"
        if ch == "," and depth == 0:
            parts.append(part)
            part = ""
        else:
            part += ch
    parts.append(part)
    names: set[str] = set()
    for declarator in parts:
        pointer = _FN_PTR_NAME_RE.search(declarator)
        if pointer:
            names.add(pointer.group(1))
            continue
        flat = re.sub(r"\([^()]*\)|\[[^\]]*\]", " ", declarator)
        idents = _IDENT_RE.findall(flat)
        if idents:
            names.add(idents[-1])
    return names


def _type_names(text: str) -> frozenset[str]:
    names = set(_TAG_RE.findall(text)) | _enumerators(text)
    if text.startswith("typedef"):
        tail = text[text.rfind("}") + 1 :] if "}" in text else text[len("typedef") :]
        names |= _declarator_names(tail.rstrip("; \t\n"))
    return frozenset(names)


def _comment_spans(source: str) -> list[tuple[int, int]]:
    return [
        match.span()
        for match in _COMMENT_OR_LITERAL_RE.finditer(source)
        if match.group("comment") is not None
    ]


class _Scan:
    """One lexical pass over a source file, shared by the recipes."""

    def __init__(self, source: str) -> None:
        self.source = source
        self.no_comments = mask_comments(source)
        self.code = _code_view(self.no_comments)
        self.items = _top_level_items(self.code)
        self.comments = _comment_spans(source)

    def function(self, symbol: str) -> tuple[_Item, int] | None:
        """The definition of `symbol` and the offset of its body's ``{``."""
        brace = find_definition_brace(self.source, symbol)
        if brace is None:
            return None
        for item in self.items:
            if item.is_function and item.brace == brace:
                return item, brace
        return None

    def target(self, symbol: str) -> tuple[_Item, int]:
        found = self.function(symbol)
        if found is None:
            raise RecipeError(f"no definition of {symbol!r} found")
        return found

    def doc_start(self, item_start: int) -> int:
        """Offset where the comment block directly above `item_start` begins.

        A comment is a doc comment only when no blank line separates it from the
        item and nothing else shares its first line; a run of ``//`` lines is one
        block. Anything else (a file header, a trailing comment on the previous
        statement) is not.
        """
        start = item_start
        for first, last in reversed([c for c in self.comments if c[1] <= item_start]):
            gap = self.source[last:start]
            line_start = self.source.rfind("\n", 0, first) + 1
            if (
                gap.strip()
                or gap.count("\n") > 1
                or self.source[line_start:first].strip()
                or (
                    start != item_start
                    and not (
                        self.source.startswith("//", first)
                        and self.source.startswith("//", start)
                    )
                )
            ):
                break
            start = first
        return start

    def definitions_used(self, seed: str) -> list[_Definition]:
        """Type/macro definitions `seed` (code text) needs, transitively."""
        defs = self._definitions()
        used = set(_IDENT_RE.findall(seed))
        selected: set[int] = set()
        changed = True
        while changed:
            changed = False
            for index, definition in enumerate(defs):
                if index not in selected and definition.names & used:
                    selected.add(index)
                    used |= definition.uses
                    changed = True

    def _definitions(self) -> list[_Definition]:
        """Type and macro definitions of the file, in source order."""
        defs: list[_Definition] = []
        for item in self.items:
            text = self.code[item.start : item.end]
            head = _IDENT_RE.match(text)
            if item.is_function or head is None or head.group() not in _TYPE_HEADS:
                continue
            names = _type_names(text)
            if names:
                defs.append(
                    _Definition(
                        item.start,
                        item.end,
                        names,
                        frozenset(_IDENT_RE.findall(text)) - names,
                        self.source[item.start : item.end],
                    )
                )
        for match in _DEFINE_RE.finditer(self.no_comments):
            text = match.group().strip()
            name = match.group(1)
            defs.append(
                _Definition(
                    match.start(),
                    match.end(),
                    frozenset({name}),
                    frozenset(_IDENT_RE.findall(text)) - {name, "define"},
                    text,
                )
            )
        return sorted(defs, key=lambda d: d.start)


def _pack(definitions: list[_Definition], target: str) -> str:
    sections = ["\n".join(d.text for d in definitions), target.strip("\n")]
    return "\n\n".join(s for s in sections if s) + "\n"

    del project_root

    for recipe in (
        Recipe("baseline", "1", _baseline),
        Recipe("sighted", "1", _sighted),
        Recipe("blind", "1", _blind),

# Design RFC 0007 — What should we prove? The property proposer at project scale

- **Status:** Draft / RFC (thinking aid — not yet an ADR)
- **Date:** 2026-10-23

## Problem

The property proposer decides *what* Forseti checks, and so it decides how much a VERIFIED is
worth. Two questions are open and should be answered by measurement, not taste:

1. **What does Forseti send the proposer?** The whole function, an interface, a description,
   a formal spec, the surrounding context — and which of these actually matter?
2. **What does the proposer send back?** Pre/postconditions, intermediate asserts, loop
   invariants, something else?

The target setting is **large existing C projects** (think the Linux kernel), where an agent
adds a new function to an existing file or modifies an existing function. Single-file kernels
are a smoke test, not the goal. This RFC designs the experiments and tooling to answer both
questions in that setting. It builds on RFC-0006 (spec quality as the positioning; equivalence
as property source S1).

## Where it is today

`semantic/v1` (`properties/prompts.py`) sends the **whole unit file** plus the symbol name
(`core/propose.py` reads the file as-is). It gets back up to 6 candidates, each
`{expression, domain, referenced_params, rationale}`: one postcondition after a single call,
plus preconditions over inputs only. Harnesses (`properties/harness.py`) take scalars,
`(ptr, len)` buffers under `--max-len`, and output buffers. They cannot express pre-state
("an in-place sort is a permutation of its input"), properties over two calls, intermediate
asserts, loop invariants, or invariants of struct arguments. `Provenance` records
`prompt_id`, `prompt_version`, `provider`, `model`.

## Ground rules

### 1. Temporal hygiene: only artifacts that existed when the code was written

Our own corpus leaks the answer to the proposer in three ways:

- every `examples/*.c` has a harness `main` whose `assert`s *are* the target properties;
- file headers describe the intended properties and the latent edge case, and the `_bug`
  twins name the staged defect (*"rb_push drops its `if (r->count == CAP)` full-check"*);
- `semantic/v1` uses `abs` as its few-shot example, so `abs.c`/`abs_fixed.c` are contaminated.

The general rule is not "strip comments". In a real project, comments such as kernel-doc are
genuine author intent and are exactly what the proposer should read. The rule is: **the context
may contain only artifacts that existed at write time.** Leaks are (a) annotations written by
us with knowledge of the answer, and (b) in history replay, anything written after the change —
the fix commit, its message, later tests, later comments. Use the *introducing* commit's code and
message, never the fix's.

### 2. Kill-rate alone rewards transcription

A proposer that reads the body and restates it as a postcondition kills nearly every mutant —
and, if the original has a bug, encodes the bug. So mutation-kill cannot be the primary metric;
**bug-pair discrimination** is (see Metrics).

### 3. A hold counts only under the verification discipline

`--unwind k --no-unwinding-assertions` gives a spurious VERIFIED for post-loop asserts when `k`
does not exceed the trip count (`examples/README.md`, roadmap Risk 1). A property "holds" only
with `k` above the trip count *and* a reachability/non-vacuity check passed. This is part of every
metric's definition, not a separate one.

## The unit of experiment: an edit event

An **edit event** is: the project snapshot at the parent commit, the diff, and the intent text
(task prompt, issue, or commit message), mapped to the functions it touches.

| | Modified function | New function |
|---|---|---|
| Previous version | yes → S1 equivalence (RFC-0006) | no |
| Accepted properties | carried forward and re-checked | none |
| Proposer's job | properties for *what changed* | properties from scratch |
| Strongest intent sources | diff, intent text, behaviour-diff witness | intent text, callers, neighbours, analogues |

For a modified function, the S1 behaviour-diff witness (input, old output, new output) is itself
a proposer input: "these inputs changed behaviour — state the new intended behaviour." Renamed,
moved and deleted functions are out of scope for v1 (see open questions).

## Inputs: a context pack, not the whole file

Whole files do not scale (kernel files run to thousands of lines) and mix intent with noise.
The proposer instead gets a **context pack**: a ranked, token-budgeted set of slices drawn from a
project index at the parent commit.

| Slice | Content | Hypothesis |
|---|---|---|
| **Target** | the function (post-edit) and its doc comment | grounding: names, domains, overflow sites |
| **Intent** | task prompt / issue / commit message | the strongest body-independent source |
| **Diff** | old vs. new, for modified functions | focuses on what changed |
| **Types** | struct/typedef/enum/macro definitions used, bounded depth | needed for struct invariants |
| **Callees** | signatures, doc comments, *existing accepted contracts* — not bodies | compositional; keeps the pack small |
| **Callers** | call sites with a few lines of context | how the result is relied on (`a[f(x)]` ⇒ `f(x) < len`) |
| **Neighbours / analogues** | sibling functions; the function a new one resembles | conventions, error-code idioms |
| **Tests** | unit tests touching the function (KUnit in the kernel) | examples to generalise (Paper A's trick) |

**Recipes** are subsets of slices, and are the experiment's input factor:

- **Baseline** — today's behaviour: the whole file, with our annotations and `main` removed.
- **Blind** — everything except the target body. It cannot transcribe the implementation.

- **Date:** 2026-10-23

## Problem

The property proposer decides *what* Forseti checks, and so it decides how much a VERIFIED is
worth. Two questions are open and should be answered by measurement, not taste:

1. **What does Forseti send the proposer?** The whole function, an interface, a description,
   a formal spec, the surrounding context — and which of these actually matter?
2. **What does the proposer send back?** Pre/postconditions, intermediate asserts, loop
   invariants, something else?

The target setting is **large existing C projects** (think the Linux kernel), where an agent
adds a new function to an existing file or modifies an existing function. Single-file kernels
are a smoke test, not the goal. This RFC designs the experiments and tooling to answer both
questions in that setting. It builds on RFC-0006 (spec quality as the positioning; equivalence
as property source S1).

## Where it is today

`semantic/v1` (`properties/prompts.py`) sends the **whole unit file** plus the symbol name
(`core/propose.py` reads the file as-is). It gets back up to 6 candidates, each
`{expression, domain, referenced_params, rationale}`: one postcondition after a single call,
plus preconditions over inputs only. Harnesses (`properties/harness.py`) take scalars,
`(ptr, len)` buffers under `--max-len`, and output buffers. They cannot express pre-state
("an in-place sort is a permutation of its input"), properties over two calls, intermediate
asserts, loop invariants, or invariants of struct arguments. `Provenance` records
`prompt_id`, `prompt_version`, `provider`, `model`.

### 1. Temporal hygiene: only artifacts that existed when the code was written

Our own corpus leaks the answer to the proposer in three ways:

- every `examples/*.c` has a harness `main` whose `assert`s *are* the target properties;
- file headers describe the intended properties and the latent edge case, and the `_bug`
  twins name the staged defect (*"rb_push drops its `if (r->count == CAP)` full-check"*);

The general rule is not "strip comments". In a real project, comments such as kernel-doc are
genuine author intent and are exactly what the proposer should read. The rule is: **the context
may contain only artifacts that existed at write time.** Leaks are (a) annotations written by
us with knowledge of the answer, and (b) in history replay, anything written after the change —
the fix commit, its message, later tests, later comments. Use the *introducing* commit's code and
message, never the fix's.

### 2. Kill-rate alone rewards transcription

A proposer that reads the body and restates it as a postcondition kills nearly every mutant —
and, if the original has a bug, encodes the bug. So mutation-kill cannot be the primary metric;
**bug-pair discrimination** is (see Metrics).

Base directory for this skill: /home/pmatos/.claude/skills/investigate

# Investigate — End-to-End GitHub Issue Workflow

Repo-agnostic workflow that takes a GitHub issue (bug **or** feature request) from
reported state to an open pull request that closes the issue. Discover project
conventions at runtime — assume no build commands, test runners, or languages.

Two execution modes:

- **Interactive** — ask the user (via AskUserQuestion) to resolve ambiguity.
- **Non-interactive** — running headlessly (`claude -p`, CI, automation). Never
  ask the user; on irreducible ambiguity, fail with a clear error rather than
  guess silently.

Treat "Can I reach the user right now?" as the deciding factor. If not, the run
is non-interactive — surface the blocker and exit.

## Bundled resources

The deterministic shell logic lives in `scripts/`; the design rationale lives in
`references/`. Invoke a script by its absolute path. When loaded as a plugin,
that path is `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/investigate/scripts/<name>`; if
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is unset (skill loaded standalone), resolve `scripts/`
relative to this SKILL.md. The examples below abbreviate the prefix as
`scripts/`.

- **`scripts/resolve-issue.sh`** — Phase 1 issue-number resolution.
- **`scripts/collect-instructions.sh`** — Phase 3.2 scoped-instruction walk over
  the changed paths' ancestors.
- **`scripts/git-safety-lib.sh`** — shared remote/default-branch resolvers
  (sourced by the two scripts below; never run directly).
- **`scripts/check-branch.sh`** — Phase 5.0 branch-safety guard.
- **`scripts/push-branch.sh`** — Phase 6 upstream-aware push.
- **`references/issue-number-resolution.md`** — Phase 1 rules, edge cases, and
  the two invariants the resolver enforces.
- **`references/scoped-instructions.md`** — Phase 3.2 precedence and merge rules,
  and why the walk is deferred until the plan's paths are known.
- **`references/git-safety.md`** — how the guard and push resolve the same
  remote and the repo's default branch, and why.

## Phase 1 — Resolve the issue number

Run the resolver, passing the raw invocation argument (empty if none):

```bash
scripts/resolve-issue.sh "${ARGUMENTS:-}"
```

It accepts `123` or `#123`, else infers the number from the branch name, then
verifies the issue exists. Act on its exit code:

- **0** — stdout is the issue number. Record it and continue.
- **2** — no number could be resolved; stdout is the current branch name.
  - Interactive: ask via AskUserQuestion — "What is the GitHub issue number to
    investigate?"
  - Non-interactive: fail with exactly this message (substitute the branch):
    ```
    investigate: no issue number provided and cannot infer from branch '<BRANCH>'. Re-run with the issue number, e.g. /investigate 123.
    ```
- **1** — hard failure (an explicit issue does not exist, or `gh` could not reach
  GitHub). The script already printed the specific message to stderr; relay it
  and abort.

The resolver deliberately never discards an explicit `/investigate <N>` silently,
and only clears a branch-inferred guess on a confirmed "not found". See
`references/issue-number-resolution.md` for the extraction rules and the
`release/2.0-issue-123` / `dependabot/...` / `pr2024` / `hotfix-1.2.3` cases.

## Phase 2 — Fetch and classify the issue

Fetch the full issue:

```bash
gh issue view "$ISSUE" --json number,title,body,labels,state,comments
```

If the issue is already closed, stop and confirm the user wants to proceed before
continuing.

Classify as **bug** or **feature**, in order:

1. **Labels (strongest signal).** Bug: `bug`, `defect`, `regression`, `crash`.
   Feature: `enhancement`, `feature`, `feature-request`, `new feature`.
2. **Title/body keywords**, if no decisive label. Bug: "expected … actual",
   "reproduce", "repro", "crash", "panic", "error", "fails", "broken",
   "regression", stack traces, version numbers. Feature: "would be nice",
   "support for", "add", "implement", "proposal", "feature request", "RFC".
3. **Still ambiguous.** Interactive: ask which workflow to follow.
   Non-interactive: default to the **bug workflow** (reproduction is harmless and
   reveals more context) and print: "Classified as bug by fallback heuristic;
   verify before merging."

Record the classification and proceed to the matching workflow.

## Phase 3 — Discover project conventions

### 3.1 Baseline (top-level) conventions

Read the project's own instructions for how to build, test, lint, and commit:

```bash
cat CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md 2>/dev/null
ls README* CONTRIBUTING*
```

Also infer the toolchain from manifests:

- `package.json` → npm/yarn/pnpm scripts (`test`, `lint`, `build`, `typecheck`).
- `Cargo.toml` → `cargo test`, `cargo clippy`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo build`.
- `pyproject.toml` / `setup.py` → `pytest`, `ruff`/`flake8`, `mypy`/`pyright`,
  plus `uv`/`hatch` if present.
- `go.mod` → `go test ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt -l`, `go build ./...`.
- `Makefile` → `test`, `lint`, `check`, `ci` targets.
- `pom.xml` / `build.gradle` → `mvn test` / `./gradlew test`.

Record the discovered test, lint/format-check, type-check, and build commands as
the *baseline* check set. Prefer a project's own canonical command sequence (from
`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md`) over the inferred defaults.

### 3.2 Scoped conventions along the changed paths

Repos with per-package or nested instructions (e.g. `frontend/AGENTS.md`) apply
extra or overriding rules to the files beneath them, so the top-level baseline
alone can miss the checks and commit rules that actually govern a change. This
step needs to know which files you will touch, so it runs **after Phase 4's plan
settles the target paths** (see 4A.4 / 4B.3), not now.

Once those paths are known, collect the instruction files along their ancestors:

```bash
scripts/collect-instructions.sh <changed-path> [<changed-path> ...]
```

It walks each path's directory up to the repo root and prints every
`CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` it finds — deduplicated (symlink-aware) and ordered
baseline (repo root) → closest (deepest). Read each file and merge with
**closest-wins** precedence: the top-level file is the baseline; a nearer file
overrides it on conflict and may add checks the baseline omits. When a scoped
file changes or adds a command relative to the baseline, surface a one-line
divergence note — which file, which command — so the validation command set is
auditable rather than silently flattened. Feed the merged command set into the
validation step (4A.6 / 4B.5).

Empty output (or exit 0 with nothing printed) means no scoped file governs the
change — fall back to the 3.1 baseline alone. See
`references/scoped-instructions.md` for the precedence rationale.

## Phase 4 — Workflow dispatch

### 4A. Bug workflow

**4A.1 Analyse.** From the issue body and comments, extract the reported vs.
expected behaviour, reproduction steps, inputs, environment notes, the affected
version, and likely subsystem(s) from file paths, error messages, or stack
traces.

**4A.2 Reproduce.** Build a *minimal* reproducer using the project's normal
commands. Confirm the bug manifests locally before changing anything — keep the
reproducer small and self-contained. When the repo has a test harness, write it
as an automated test: that test is the red step of the test-first policy below,
not a throwaway to be replaced later. If the
bug cannot be reproduced, document the gaps. Interactive: ask for clarification.
Non-interactive: comment on the issue describing what was tried and what failed,
then exit documenting the blocker.

**4A.3 Locate.** Use `grep`/`rg` for error strings, function names, and log
messages from the repro, then read the suspects. For non-trivial bugs (multiple
files, subtle root cause), delegate to `/pm-plan` with a focused prompt
describing the bug, the repro, and the symptom.

**4A.4 Plan the fix.** Write a concise numbered plan, each step citing `file:line`
targets and the change to make (or use the `/pm-plan` output). Convert the plan to
a task list with **TaskCreate** before executing — one task per reviewable unit.
Once the target paths are settled, run Phase 3.2 (`scripts/collect-instructions.sh`)
over them and fold the merged, closest-wins check set into the plan. List the
test file path(s) alongside the production targets so 3.2 covers both.

**4A.5 Fix (best effort).** Apply the changes under the test-first policy
below, starting from the 4A.2 test. Mark each task `in_progress`
when starting it and `completed` the moment it is done — do not batch updates. On
hitting a wall (mismatched assumptions, scope explosion, blocked by another bug),
surface it: interactive — ask how to proceed; non-interactive — comment on the
issue, leave the partial branch, exit. **Do not** open a half-finished PR.

**4A.6 Validate.** Run the merged check set from Phase 3 (the 3.1 baseline plus
any 3.2 scoped instructions) in order — format/format-check, lint, type-check,
tests, build — stopping and iterating on any failure. Loop until all are green,
then proceed to Phase 5.

### 4B. Feature workflow

**4B.1 Explore.** Map the parts of the codebase the feature touches. Read the
relevant modules, study existing patterns (naming, layering, error handling, test
style), and note the conventions to mirror. For non-trivial features (multiple
modules, new abstractions, data-model changes), delegate to `/pm-plan` and treat
its output as the master plan.

**4B.2 Resolve design questions.** For any genuinely ambiguous decision (data
model, API shape, UX, where the feature lives):

- Interactive: stress-test the design with the user. Use `/grill-with-docs` (or
  the simpler `/grill-me`) if available; otherwise list the open questions and
  resolve each via AskUserQuestion before writing code. Update the plan with the
  answers.
- Non-interactive: if the design is ambiguous, fail with exactly this message
  (substitute the issue number):
  ```
  investigate: feature request #<N> is ambiguous and cannot be designed non-interactively. Provide more details or run interactively.
  ```
  `/pm-plan` answers its own questions headlessly, so a guess on one of these
  decisions recorded in its `## Assumptions` section counts as ambiguous.

If the request is concrete enough that no design choices remain open (e.g. "add a
`--quiet` flag that suppresses progress output"), proceed without a design pass.

**4B.3 Plan.** As in 4A.4 — concise `file:line` step list, including test file
paths, converted to a TaskCreate task list before execution (or the `/pm-plan`
output).

**4B.4 Implement (best effort).** Follow the repo norms from 4B.1. Build testable
behaviour under the test-first policy below, one failing test per behaviour.
Mark tasks `in_progress`/`completed` as work progresses. Same blocker rules as 4A.5 — surface (interactive) or comment and
exit (non-interactive); no half-finished PRs.

**4B.5 Validate.** As in 4A.6 — run the merged check set (Phase 3.1 baseline plus
3.2 scoped) in order; loop until green.

### Test-first policy

Applies to 4A.5 and 4B.4. The practice is the default; `/tdd` is the preferred
vehicle for it, and without `/tdd` the manual loop is the same: write the
failing test, confirm it fails, then write the implementation.

- **Red, then green.** Write the failing test before the fix, run it, and
  confirm it fails for the reported reason. Make it pass with the smallest
  change, then refactor while green.
- **Testability changes come first.** If the test cannot be written without a
  production edit (exporting a private function, extracting a seam, injecting a
  dependency, adding an entry point), make that minimal, behaviour-preserving
  change first and keep it separate from the fix.
- **A bad red step goes back to 4A.2.** A test that passes immediately, or fails
  for another reason (setup, import, unrelated assertion), has not reproduced
  the bug. Fix the test, or take the 4A.2 cannot-reproduce path. Never weaken a
  test until it fails.
- **Non-interactive runs do not re-confirm seams.** `/tdd` asks the user to
  confirm the seams under test. With no user, the seam is the one the 4A.2
  reproducer or the 4A.4/4B.3 plan already identified; treat it as pre-agreed.

**When test-first does not fit.** Skip it, and record the reason in the PR body
(the test-plan line in Phase 6), when any of these hold:

- No usable test harness, or the code is out of the suite's reach (shell glue,
  build scripts, installers). Do not build a test framework to satisfy the
  policy.
- The change is docs, prose, config, build, CI or packaging, where there is
  nothing to assert or running the pipeline is the test.
- The failure is non-deterministic (races, timing, flakiness), so a failing test
  proves little.
- It needs real hardware, a specific OS, production data, or an external service
  that is unavailable.
- The fix is a dependency bump or vendored patch, so a test would exercise the
  library rather than this repo.
- It is a performance regression; use a benchmark with a threshold instead.
- It is a pure refactor or deletion; the existing tests are the safety net.
- It is a visual or UI defect that only a screenshot or manual check confirms.

Fall back to the best available check: the manual repro from 4A.2, or a
before/after run of the relevant command, with the output summarised in the PR
body. The fallback never blocks the fix.

## Phase 5 — Commit

### Step 5.0 — Branch safety guard

Before any `git add`, `git commit`, or `git push`, verify the worktree is on a
topic branch — never the repo's default branch (whatever its name) and never a
detached HEAD:

```bash
scripts/check-branch.sh
```

Act on its exit code:

- **0** — safe (topic branch, or the default branch could not be resolved but HEAD
  is not detached). Proceed to Step 5.1.
- **5** — refuse. stdout is the offending branch name (or `detached HEAD`).
  - Interactive: ask (AskUserQuestion) which topic branch to use. `git switch
    <name>` for an existing branch or `git switch -c <name>` for a new one, then
    re-run this guard.
  - Non-interactive: fail with exactly this message (substitute the stdout value)
    and exit without committing or pushing:
    ```
    investigate: refusing to commit/push from '<BRANCH-or-detached>'. Re-run on a topic branch (e.g. issue<N>) or pass the branch explicitly.
    ```

This guards the common case of `/investigate` being invoked while still on the
default branch after the last PR merged. The guard resolves the remote and
default branch through `scripts/git-safety-lib.sh` — the same resolvers Phase 6
uses to push, so the two cannot disagree. See `references/git-safety.md`.

### Step 5.1 — Commit

Study the repo's commit style and match it:

```bash
git log --oneline -20
```

Most projects use Conventional Commits (`fix: <desc> (#N)` / `feat: <desc> (#N)`)
or free-form (`Fix <desc> (#N)` / `Add <desc> (#N)`). Whatever the style, the
subject **must reference the issue** with `(#N)`. Add a one-line body on *why*,
not *what*, when useful.

**Authorship rule.** Check the active git identity:

```bash
git config user.email
```

If it is `pmatos@igalia.com`, commit messages and PR bodies **must not** mention
Claude, AI, "co-authored-by Claude", or generation tooling. (This rule lives in
the user's global CLAUDE.md and supersedes default behaviour.)

Stage only the changed files (avoid `git add -A`), then commit:

```bash
git add <files>
git commit -m "<message>"
```

If a pre-commit hook fails, fix the underlying issue and create a **new** commit —
never `--no-verify`, never `--amend` over a failed hook.

## Phase 6 — Push and open the PR

Push the branch, honoring any existing upstream instead of hardcoding `origin`:

```bash
scripts/push-branch.sh
```

It first-pushes with `-u` on the remote resolved by `git-safety-lib.sh`, or does a
bare `git push` if the branch already has an upstream. This matters for fork
workflows and repos whose only remote is not `origin`. See `references/git-safety.md`.

Open a PR with `gh pr create`. The body **must** contain a closing keyword so
GitHub auto-closes the issue on merge — `Closes #N`, `Fixes #N` (preferred for
bugs), or `Resolves #N`. Invoke via HEREDOC to preserve formatting:

```bash
gh pr create --title "<title>" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Summary

- <1–3 bullets on what changed and why>

Fixes #<N>

## Test plan

- [ ] <discovered test command> — all passing
- [ ] <discovered lint command> — clean
- [ ] <discovered type-check command> — clean
- [ ] Manual repro confirms the bug is fixed   (bug workflow only)
- [ ] Tests written first and seen failing — or: skipped because <reason>
EOF
)"
```

Mirror the commit subject in the PR title (minus the `(#N)` suffix — GitHub adds
the PR number). Return the PR URL to the user.

## Phase 7 — Post-PR

1. Post a friendly pointer on the issue (GitHub also links it via the closing
   keyword):
   ```bash
   gh issue comment "$ISSUE" --body "Opened PR <URL> to address this. Will auto-close on merge."
   ```
2. Do **not** close the issue manually — let the merged PR close it via the
   keyword, so a rejected PR leaves the issue open without intervention.
3. Report the PR URL and the test-plan checklist to the user.

## Supporting skills

Use if available in the active session; otherwise fall back to the per-step
alternative:

- **`/pm-plan`** — deep, multi-phase planning for non-trivial bugs or features.
  Fallback: write the plan directly with TaskCreate.
- **`/grill-with-docs`** (or `/grill-me`) — interactive design stress-test for
  ambiguous feature decisions. Fallback: a short AskUserQuestion-driven design
  pass before implementation.
- **`/tdd`** — red-green-refactor loop; the default way to implement 4A.5 and
  4B.4. Fallback: write the failing test, confirm it fails, then write the
  implementation, manually.

## Failure modes (quick reference)

Each row points to the phase that owns the exact behaviour and message — no
message is duplicated here, to keep the single source of truth in one place.

| Situation | Handled in |
|-----------|------------|
| No issue number; branch unparseable | Phase 1, exit 2 |
| Explicit issue does not exist, or `gh` unreachable | Phase 1, exit 1 (message from `resolve-issue.sh`) |
| Issue already closed | Phase 2 — stop and confirm |
| Bug cannot be reproduced | Phase 4A.2 — ask, or comment on the issue and exit |
| Feature ambiguous, non-interactive | Phase 4B.2 |
| Red test passes at once or fails for another reason | Test-first policy — back to 4A.2 |
| On the default branch or detached HEAD | Phase 5.0, exit 5 |
| Pre-commit hook fails | Phase 5.1 — fix and re-commit; never `--no-verify` |
| Validation cannot be made green | Phase 4A.6 / 4B.5 — surface or comment and exit; do not open the PR |

"""The `path::symbol` unit-id string convention, owned in one place.

A verification unit is keyed `<path>::<symbol>` (ADR-0009): a source path and the
symbol of the function within it. ~10 producers used to hand-format that with an
f-string and one consumer re-parsed it with a bare `split`, so the join and split
rules could drift with nothing to enforce them. This leaf owns them: `make_unit_id`
joins, `unit_id_symbol` recovers the symbol, `unit_id_prefix` builds the
"every unit under this path" match prefix.

Scope is the `::` separator only. This module deliberately does **not** normalize or
validate the path: each producer keeps its own left-operand spelling — Core's raw
unnormalized `source`, the Claude gate's `..`-resolved relative `rel`
(`forseti_gate.unit_id()`), oh_my_pi's own path — so every produced string is
byte-identical to the historical `f"{path}::{symbol}"` and every on-disk store key
is unchanged. A `path` is assumed to be `::`-free (every real producer passes a
filesystem path); that is what makes the round-trip hold and is not checked here.

Stdlib-only and free of `forseti` imports so it stays a dependency-free leaf that
every tier can import without a cycle and without dragging heavier packages into
the latency-sensitive hooks.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

_SEP = "::"


def make_unit_id(path: str | os.PathLike[str], symbol: str) -> str:
    """Join an already-spelled `path` and `symbol` into ``<path>::<symbol>``.

    Byte-identical to the historical ``f"{path}::{symbol}"`` — the same ``str``
    interpolation, never ``os.fspath``, so a `Path` left operand stringifies exactly
    as it did before. `path` is taken verbatim: no normalization, no ``..``
    resolution. `symbol` may be the ``?`` sentinel used for an unknown symbol.
    """
    return f"{path}{_SEP}{symbol}"


def unit_id_symbol(unit_id: str) -> str:
    """The symbol half of `unit_id`: everything after the FIRST ``::``.

    Splitting on the first separator lets a C++ ``p::Foo::bar`` keep ``Foo::bar`` as
    its symbol. A string with no ``::`` is returned unchanged — the silent
    malformed-id fallback the sole consumer already relied on, where a
    separator-less id reads as all-symbol.
    """
    return unit_id.split(_SEP, 1)[1] if _SEP in unit_id else unit_id


def unit_id_prefix(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> str:
    """The ``<path>::`` prefix shared by every unit id under `path`.

    Equal to ``make_unit_id(path, "")``; a `unit_id.startswith(unit_id_prefix(path))`
    test selects the ids that belong to one source file.
    """
    return make_unit_id(path, "")
    from .prompts import PromptTemplate
    from .store import PropertyStore


class CandidateStore(Protocol):
    """The store subset the proposer persists into (real `PropertyStore` fits).

    Structural: only the two members the proposer touches, so tests inject a
    dict-backed fake and #62's concrete store need not be built to exercise #65.
    """

    def get(self, property_id: str) -> Property | None: ...

    def add(self, prop: Property) -> None: ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProposalRequest:
    """One unit to propose properties for: its id, source, prompt, and signature.

    `signature` is caller-supplied (parsed via `extract_signature` or hand-built):
    when present it unlocks the identifier/parameter checks and the renderability
    gate; when `None` those are skipped and only the source-free static checks
    apply. `source_text` must be a main-free kernel slice -- the same text the
    harness writer inlines. `context`, when present (a recipe's output, #388),
    is what the prompt shows the model instead of `source_text`.
    """

    unit_id: str
    source_text: str
    prompt: PromptTemplate = DEFAULT_PROMPT
    signature: UnitSignature | None = None
    context: ProposalContext | None = None

    @property
    def symbol(self) -> str:
        """The function name -- the ``symbol`` half of ``path::symbol``."""
        return unit_id_symbol(self.unit_id)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CandidateSpec:
    """One parsed model candidate, before validation.

    Mirrors the JSON contract the prompt asks for. `kind` is captured only so a
    stray non-semantic candidate can be rejected (ADR-0009 D2); the prompt never
    asks for it, so it is usually `None`.
    """

    expression: str
    domain: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    referenced_params: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    rationale: str = ""
    kind: str | None = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RejectedCandidate:
    """A parsed candidate that failed a static check, with the reason it failed.

    Rejections are *returned*, not raised: a bad candidate is data about the
    model's output, not an error in the proposer.
    """

    spec: CandidateSpec
    reason: str

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "expression": self.spec.expression,
            "domain": list(self.spec.domain),
            "reason": self.reason,
        }


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProposalResult:
    """The outcome of one proposer run: accepted properties, rejects, provenance.

    `to_dict` is the JSON shape #44 serialises (mirrors `core/verify.py`'s
    payload style). `provider`/`model` record the backend for telemetry; the
    persisted `Property.provenance` carries only prompt id/version by design.
    """

    unit_id: str
    prompt_id: str

(`forseti_gate.unit_id()`), oh_my_pi's own path — so every produced string is
byte-identical to the historical `f"{path}::{symbol}"` and every on-disk store key
is unchanged. A `path` is assumed to be `::`-free (every real producer passes a
filesystem path); that is what makes the round-trip hold and is not checked here.

Stdlib-only and free of `forseti` imports so it stays a dependency-free leaf that
every tier can import without a cycle and without dragging heavier packages into
the latency-sensitive hooks.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import os

_SEP = "::"


def make_unit_id(path: str | os.PathLike[str], symbol: str) -> str:
    """Join an already-spelled `path` and `symbol` into ``<path>::<symbol>``.

    Byte-identical to the historical ``f"{path}::{symbol}"`` — the same ``str``
    interpolation, never ``os.fspath``, so a `Path` left operand stringifies exactly
    as it did before. `path` is taken verbatim: no normalization, no ``..``
    resolution. `symbol` may be the ``?`` sentinel used for an unknown symbol.
    """
    return f"{path}{_SEP}{symbol}"


def unit_id_symbol(unit_id: str) -> str:
    """The symbol half of `unit_id`: everything after the FIRST ``::``.

    Splitting on the first separator lets a C++ ``p::Foo::bar`` keep ``Foo::bar`` as
    its symbol. A string with no ``::`` is returned unchanged — the silent
    malformed-id fallback the sole consumer already relied on, where a
    separator-less id reads as all-symbol.
    """
    return unit_id.split(_SEP, 1)[1] if _SEP in unit_id else unit_id


def unit_id_prefix(path: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> str:
    """The ``<path>::`` prefix shared by every unit id under `path`.

    Equal to ``make_unit_id(path, "")``; a `unit_id.startswith(unit_id_prefix(path))`
    test selects the ids that belong to one source file.
    """
    return make_unit_id(path, "")
    from .prompts import PromptTemplate

class CandidateStore(Protocol):
    """The store subset the proposer persists into (real `PropertyStore` fits).

    Structural: only the two members the proposer touches, so tests inject a
    dict-backed fake and #62's concrete store need not be built to exercise #65.
    """

    def get(self, property_id: str) -> Property | None: ...

    def add(self, prop: Property) -> None: ...


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProposalRequest:
    """One unit to propose properties for: its id, source, prompt, and signature.

    `signature` is caller-supplied (parsed via `extract_signature` or hand-built):
    when present it unlocks the identifier/parameter checks and the renderability
    gate; when `None` those are skipped and only the source-free static checks
    apply. `source_text` must be a main-free kernel slice -- the same text the
    harness writer inlines. `context`, when present (a recipe's output, #388),
    is what the prompt shows the model instead of `source_text`.
    """

    unit_id: str
    source_text: str
    prompt: PromptTemplate = DEFAULT_PROMPT
    signature: UnitSignature | None = None
    context: ProposalContext | None = None

    @property
    def symbol(self) -> str:
        """The function name -- the ``symbol`` half of ``path::symbol``."""
        return unit_id_symbol(self.unit_id)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CandidateSpec:
    """One parsed model candidate, before validation.

    Mirrors the JSON contract the prompt asks for. `kind` is captured only so a
    stray non-semantic candidate can be rejected (ADR-0009 D2); the prompt never
    asks for it, so it is usually `None`.
    """

    expression: str
    domain: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    referenced_params: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    rationale: str = ""
    kind: str | None = None


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RejectedCandidate:
    """A parsed candidate that failed a static check, with the reason it failed.

    Rejections are *returned*, not raised: a bad candidate is data about the
    model's output, not an error in the proposer.
    """

    spec: CandidateSpec
    reason: str

    def to_dict(self) -> dict[str, object]:
        return {
            "expression": self.spec.expression,
            "domain": list(self.spec.domain),
            "reason": self.reason,
        }


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ProposalResult:
    """The outcome of one proposer run: accepted properties, rejects, provenance.

    `to_dict` is the JSON shape #44 serialises (mirrors `core/verify.py`'s
    payload style). `provider`/`model` record the backend for telemetry; the

proposer continues to accept requests built from in-memory source and signatures.

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

from forseti.properties import (
    HarnessError,
    PromptTemplate,
    ProposalRequest,
    build_context,

from forseti.properties.prompts import DEFAULT_PROMPT
from forseti.unit_id import make_unit_id


def prepare_proposal_request(
    source: Path,
    *,
    function: str,
    prompt: PromptTemplate = DEFAULT_PROMPT,
    recipe: str | None = None,
    project_root: Path = Path(),
) -> ProposalRequest:
    """Read once and prepare a request, preserving source text and path spelling.

    Only an unsupported signature (`HarnessError`) degrades to signature-free
    validation. File-read failures and unexpected parser errors propagate. Every
    invocation reads afresh; callers submitting a batch prepare before its loop.
    `recipe` names an input recipe (`forseti.properties.recipes`) whose context the
    prompt shows instead of the whole file (`RecipeError` if it cannot be built);
    `None` keeps the whole-file prompt.
    """
    source_text = source.read_text()
    unit_id = make_unit_id(source, function)
    try:
        signature = extract_signature(source_text, function)
    except HarnessError:
        signature = None
    context = (
        None
        if recipe is None
        else build_context(
            recipe,
            unit_id=unit_id,
            source_text=source_text,
            project_root=project_root,
        )
    )
    return ProposalRequest(
        unit_id=unit_id,
        source_text=source_text,
        prompt=prompt,
        signature=signature,
        context=context,
    )

typedef int (*visit_fn)(int);

[project]
name = "forseti"
version = "1.11.0"
description = "ESBMC-in-the-loop: write -> verify -> counterexample -> fix"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
# The MCP server (forseti.core.mcp_server) needs the MCP SDK; kept optional so
# the base install and the loop/esbmc path stay dependency-free. Pinned to the
# MCPServer-supporting range: mcp 2.0.0 renamed mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP to
# mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, so a loose >=1.0 could install an SDK where
# `from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer` fails.
mcp = ["mcp>=2.3.0,<3"]
# dev pulls in the mcp extra so CI type-checks and tests the server too.
dev = [
    "build>=1.6.1",
    "setuptools>=84.2.1",
    "pytest>=9.1.1",
    "pytest-cov>=7.1.0",
    "hypothesis>=6.170.12",
    "ty>=0.0.92",
    "ruff>=0.17.2",
    "forseti[mcp]",
]

[project.scripts]
forseti = "forseti.core.cli:main"
forseti-esbmc = "forseti.esbmc.cli:main"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["src"]
testpaths = ["tests"]

[tool.ruff]
target-version = "py312"
line-length = 88

[tool.ruff.lint]
# E/F: pycodestyle + pyflakes; I: import sorting; B: bugbear; UP: pyupgrade;
# SIM: simplify; RUF: ruff-native; ANN: every def must be annotated -- ty (our
# type checker) has no `strict = true`-equivalent annotation-completeness
# rule of its own, so this is what stands in for that half of what mypy strict
# used to enforce. `from __future__ import annotations` is used throughout, so
# UP/I are near no-ops.
select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "SIM", "RUF", "ANN"]
# ANN401 (`Any` in an annotation) is a deliberate, common choice in this
# codebase (e.g. JSON payloads, **kwargs forwarding) -- not the "annotations
# exist" property ANN otherwise enforces.
ignore = ["ANN401"]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["forseti"]
branch = true
# `python -m forseti.core` shims: a docstring, an import, and a __main__ guard
# that by construction only runs out-of-process. Nothing to assert, and their
# permanent 0% would otherwise eat ~0.3pp of the 95% gate.
omit = ["*/__main__.py"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
# `case _: assert_never(x)` closes an exhaustive match over an Enum/Literal for
# ty's benefit; by construction the match already covers every member, so the
# wildcard clause can never run and its permanent 0% is noise, not a gap.
exclude_also = ['if __name__ == "__main__":', "case _:\\s*$"]
# Load-bearing, not cosmetic: coverage.py's fail-under test is
# `round(total, precision) < fail_under`, and precision defaults to 0. At the
# default, 95.5-95.99% rounds to 96 and passes `--cov-fail-under=96` — pytest-cov
# even prints "FAIL ... Total coverage: 95.65%" and still exits 0. 2 makes the
# gate mean what it says, and matches codecov.yml's own precision.
precision = 2

requires = ["setuptools>=84.2.1"]

[project]
name = "forseti"
version = "1.11.0"
description = "ESBMC-in-the-loop: write -> verify -> counterexample -> fix"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = []

[project.optional-dependencies]
# The MCP server (forseti.core.mcp_server) needs the MCP SDK; kept optional so
# the base install and the loop/esbmc path stay dependency-free. Pinned to the
# MCPServer-supporting range: mcp 2.0.0 renamed mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP to
# mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, so a loose >=1.0 could install an SDK where
# `from mcp.server.mcpserver import MCPServer` fails.
mcp = ["mcp>=2.3.0,<3"]
# dev pulls in the mcp extra so CI type-checks and tests the server too.
dev = [
    "build>=1.6.1",
    "setuptools>=84.2.1",
    "pytest>=9.1.1",
    "pytest-cov>=7.1.0",
    "hypothesis>=6.170.12",
    "ty>=0.0.92",
    "ruff>=0.17.2",
    "forseti[mcp]",
]

[project.scripts]
forseti = "forseti.core.cli:main"
forseti-esbmc = "forseti.esbmc.cli:main"

[tool.setuptools.packages.find]
where = ["src"]

[tool.pytest.ini_options]
pythonpath = ["src"]
testpaths = ["tests"]

[tool.ruff]
target-version = "py312"
line-length = 88

[tool.ruff.lint]
# E/F: pycodestyle + pyflakes; I: import sorting; B: bugbear; UP: pyupgrade;
# SIM: simplify; RUF: ruff-native; ANN: every def must be annotated -- ty (our
# type checker) has no `strict = true`-equivalent annotation-completeness
# rule of its own, so this is what stands in for that half of what mypy strict
# used to enforce. `from __future__ import annotations` is used throughout, so
# UP/I are near no-ops.
select = ["E", "F", "I", "B", "UP", "SIM", "RUF", "ANN"]
# ANN401 (`Any` in an annotation) is a deliberate, common choice in this
# codebase (e.g. JSON payloads, **kwargs forwarding) -- not the "annotations
# exist" property ANN otherwise enforces.
ignore = ["ANN401"]

[tool.coverage.run]
source = ["forseti"]
branch = true
# `python -m forseti.core` shims: a docstring, an import, and a __main__ guard
# that by construction only runs out-of-process. Nothing to assert, and their
# permanent 0% would otherwise eat ~0.3pp of the 95% gate.
omit = ["*/__main__.py"]

[tool.coverage.report]
show_missing = true
# `case _: assert_never(x)` closes an exhaustive match over an Enum/Literal for
# ty's benefit; by construction the match already covers every member, so the
# wildcard clause can never run and its permanent 0% is noise, not a gap.
exclude_also = ['if __name__ == "__main__":', "case _:\\s*$"]
# Load-bearing, not cosmetic: coverage.py's fail-under test is
# `round(total, precision) < fail_under`, and precision defaults to 0. At the
# default, 95.5-95.99% rounds to 96 and passes `--cov-fail-under=96` — pytest-cov
# even prints "FAIL ... Total coverage: 95.65%" and still exits 0. 2 makes the
# gate mean what it says, and matches codecov.yml's own precision.
precision = 2

"""Tests for the SQLite property store: round-trips, transitions, durability."""

from __future__ import annotations

import dataclasses
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import pytest

from forseti.properties import (
    DuplicateProperty,
    Grading,
    GradingRequired,
    GradingVerdict,
    InvalidStatusTransition,
    Property,
    PropertyKind,
    PropertyNotFound,
    PropertyStatus,
    PropertyStore,
    Provenance,
    WrongPropertyKind,
    make_invariant,
    make_property_id,
)

HELD_HALF = Grading(GradingVerdict.HELD, 0.5, "killed 1/2; survived: m")


def make_prop(
    *,
    unit_id: str = "examples/abs.c::my_abs",
    kind: PropertyKind = PropertyKind.SEMANTIC,
    expression: str = "result >= 0",
    domain: tuple[str, ...] = ("x > INT64_MIN",),
    status: PropertyStatus = PropertyStatus.CANDIDATE,
    grading: Grading | None = None,
    description: str | None = None,
) -> Property:
    return Property(
        property_id=make_property_id(unit_id, kind, expression, domain),
        unit_id=unit_id,
        kind=kind,
        expression=expression,
        status=status,
        provenance=Provenance("proposer-v1", "1"),
        domain=domain,
        grading=grading,
        description=description,
    )


def mem_store() -> PropertyStore:
    return PropertyStore(sqlite3.connect(":memory:"))


def test_open_creates_db_file(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    store = PropertyStore.open(root=tmp_path)
    try:
        assert (tmp_path / "forseti.db").is_file()
    finally:
        store.close()
    # a second open on the same root is fine (schema is idempotent).
    PropertyStore.open(root=tmp_path).close()


def test_open_creates_missing_parent_dir(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    nested = tmp_path / "a" / "b"
    PropertyStore.open(root=nested).close()
    assert (nested / "forseti.db").is_file()


def test_add_get_roundtrip_without_grading() -> None:
    store = mem_store()
    prop = make_prop(description="abs non-negative")
    store.add(prop)
    assert store.get(prop.property_id) == prop
